description: Equipo de estudiantes de la USAL que va a quemar hasta los cimientos de la programación.
summary: Sol a Sol is a free web game for 7 to 12-year-olds. You manage a base at the lunar South Pole during the real solar storm from May 1 to 21, 2024, using NASA data (DONKI and RadLab). Every morning you allocate power between the antenna, the farm, and the shield. You spend your Forces on planting, fixing breakdowns (three minigames), upgrading buildings, or going out with the Rover. At night, you will find out if you protected yourself in time from the radiation that the LRO spacecraft actually measured near the Moon. No decision is free. Each piece of data states whether it is LIVE, ARCHIVED, SIMULATED, or CALCULATED, and the final report explains why things happened the way they did. To play, open the repository's GitHub Pages link. To collaborate on the code, see the local development instructions above.
details:
"Sol a Sol" is a web-based space survival and resource management simulator where players control a single astronaut managing a lunar outpost. The gameplay revolves around a day-and-night cycle and a dual-economy system: Base Energy (generated by the Life Support module) and Astronaut Stamina. During the day, players must make critical trade-offs—such as spending stamina to fix solar panels, allocating energy to charge radiation shields, or driving a rover (in a 2D auto-runner mini-game) to gather materials. At night, the game calculates the consequences of these choices, applying radiation damage, food consumption, and health regeneration based on real space weather conditions.

It translates complex space engineering challenges into intuitive, hands-on gameplay. Instead of passively reading about deep-space constraints, children experience the authentic tension of resource scarcity. They learn that no decision in space is free—sacrificing tonight's shield charge for an extra research trip teaches them the real-life consequences and risk-management strategies that actual astronauts and mission planners navigate.

The project aims to foster STEM vocations by inspiring the next generation of scientists, engineers, and astronauts. By making real NASA data interactive and accessible, it transforms abstract astronomical concepts into a tangible, thrilling experience, showing younger audiences that space exploration is about resilience, strategy, and critical thinking.

  • Frontend: React.js for the UI and state management, CSS3 (using radial gradients and SVGs) for lightweight visual rendering without heavy textures, and HTML5 Canvas for the dynamic rover mini-game.
  • Backend: Node.js and Express.js to fetch, process, and serve data to the client.
  • APIs & Data: NASA DONKI API (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information) for CMEs and solar flares, and NASA OSDR (Open Science Data Repository) for authentic biological constraints like plant growth in lunar regolith.

The project creatively repurposes raw, highly technical astronomical telemetry into direct gameplay mechanics. Instead of using random number generators (RNG) to create in-game disasters, the actual Sun acts as the "game master." Real solar flares and coronal mass ejections dictate the in-game radiation damage multipliers and base malfunctions. Furthermore, it cleverly disguises complex mathematics behind an age-appropriate UI featuring simple action points and health hearts, making deep-space science digestible for kids.

  • Accessibility and Audience: We tailored the complexity for 7 to 12-year-olds by separating the economy into two easily understandable metrics (Base Energy and Stamina) and using visual cues rather than heavy text.
  • Low Barrier to Entry: We built a lightweight web application that requires no downloads, accounts, or high-end hardware, making it easily adoptable in classroom settings.
  • Reliability: We implemented an offline data fallback featuring the historic May 2024 solar storms. This ensures the game remains challenging and educational even if live API calls fail or the sun is inactive on the day of gameplay.
  • Scientific Authenticity: We ensured that necessary gameplay simplifications (like merging air and water into a single "Life Support" module) still faithfully represented the core lesson of mission constraints and interdependent systems.
